title: Ambrose and the emperor
hookLine: after a massacre, Ambrose makes the emperor do public penance

lines: THE EMPEROR EXPECTS MASS AS USUAL.
cards: A letter, written by hand, meant for one reader. The reader is the emperor Theodosius, a Christian, and a man who comes to church in Milan. The writer is the bishop of Milan, Ambrose.
Something terrible has happened in the city of Thessalonica. After a riot there, the emperor's soldiers turned on the people of the city and killed them. The emperor is expected at Mass as usual.
And the bishop has to decide what to say to him.

teach.h: A PRIVATE LETTER, NOT A PUBLIC FIGHT.
teach.b: Ambrose's letter is quieter than the legend. He doesn't denounce the emperor from the pulpit. He writes privately, and he writes as a pastor.
He grieves over Thessalonica. He tells Theodosius plainly that he dare not offer the sacrifice of the Mass if the emperor intends to be there, not with this on his hands.
And he points him to someone the emperor would know from scripture: King David. After David sent a man to his death, the prophet Nathan confronted him, and David didn't argue.
In the Douay-Rheims: "And David said to Nathan: I have sinned against the Lord." Ambrose's message, more or less: a king did this before you. You can do it too.
And Theodosius did. Ambrose describes it later, in the sermon he preached at the emperor's funeral.

teach.h: THE EMPEROR LAYS ASIDE HIS RANK.
teach.b: The emperor laid aside the signs of his royal rank, wept for his sin openly in church, and asked for pardon. Public penance, done by an emperor.

teach.h: THE STORY GROWS IN THE RETELLING.

teach.b: A later historian, Theodoret, tells a more dramatic version: Ambrose meets the emperor at the church door and blocks his way in front of everyone. Ambrose's own letter is private and patient.
Both versions agree on the ending, though. The emperor stood among sinners and asked for mercy.

how: Catholics confess serious sin in the sacrament of penance, also called reconciliation; public penance like the emperor's belongs to the early Church, and today the sacrament is ordinarily private, between penitent and priest.

o: Latin for penance, sorrow shown for a sin
Latin for the pardon a bishop gives a king
Latin for a prison sentence served for a crime

games.q: the bishop and the emperor — tap the pairs.
p: laid aside his rank and wept
I have sinned against the Lord

s: Ambrose's own letter publicly shames the emperor
it's private and pastoral: it urges penance and says he can't offer Mass with the emperor present.
Ambrose points the emperor to King David's repentance
David, confronted by Nathan, said: I have sinned against the Lord.
the church-door scene comes from Ambrose himself
it comes from a later historian, Theodoret. Ambrose's own letter is quieter.

games.q: you're the bishop. the emperor's soldiers have massacred a city, and he expects to come to Mass as usual. what do you do?
o: write to him privately, urge penance, and say you can't offer Mass with him there.
denounce him by name from the pulpit.
games.why: Ambrose wrote privately, pointed him to David, and held back the Mass. the emperor did public penance.

practice: Think of someone with more power than you who needs to hear something true: a manager, an official, a landlord, someone older in the family.

Shape the one sentence you'd say, with the anger taken out and the truth kept in, and notice Ambrose's way: privately first, with respect, leaving room to change. If you pray, pray for that person by name.

wordCard.voice: paenitentia. Latin for penance, what Ambrose asked of Theodosius after the massacre at Thessalonica, before the emperor could return to Mass. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: penance, repentance — what Ambrose asked of the emperor.
